newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: NATO ministers discuss enlargement candidates.
newsitem.headline: NATO ministers discuss enlargement candidates.

text.p: NATO foreign ministers, fresh from clinching a landmark security pact with Russia, met on Thursday to start selecting which former Warsaw pact countries should be invited to join the alliance next July.

The meeting in the historic Portuguese town of Sintra will also review efforts to overhaul the alliance's outdated Cold War command structure and boost partnership programmes for countries which fail to gain alliance admittance.

"Our meetings in Sintra demonstrate that NATO is well on track for the 21st century. The Atlantic Alliance, together with its partners, remains determined to meet the challenges of the new era," NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana told the opening session.

Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to be invited to join the alliance in Madrid next month, but Romania and Slovenia -- strongly backed by some of the current 16 alliance members -- are also pushing hard.
U.S. officials say Secretary of State Madeleine Albright goes into the talks representing a U.S. position in favour of inviting three rather than five.

NATO diplomats say the largest alliance countries, mindful of the political implications of effectively committing their troops to defend other states, tend to favour a limited enlargement, at least for now.
"Britain, France and the United States are very aware of the historical factors that created the alliance and lean towards moving slowly," said one alliance envoy.
Some countries however, using the argument that the alliance is evolving from a defence union into a continent-wide security organisation, want to spread membership more widely.
"In the end, the alliance operates by consensus, and caution will probably win out," added the envoy.
NATO officials say no decision will be taken at the closed-door Sintra meeting, but for the first time countries will state their preferences openly.
"We will be searching for a consensus," said one NATO official.
He said Solana would undertake a visit of applicant countries' capitals to inform them formally of NATO's decision in the two weeks before the meeting in Madrid on July 8-9.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said the meeting would play a key role in preparing a successful Madrid summit.
"It would be strange that now we have solved the central questions, we cannot make progress on these inner questions," he told reporters when arriving for the meeting.

The Sintra meeting comes two days after NATO agreed a landmark pact with Russia, giving Moscow a key role in an emerging post-Cold War European security system and effectively removing its opposition to at least a limited alliance enlargement.
But Russia has since made clear it would still balk at former Soviet Republics winning membership of the organisation which won the Cold War without a shot being fired.

NATO countries, keen to avoid new divisions in Europe between former communist countries from central and eastern Europe, also intend to use the meeting to launch a much-improved Partnership for Peace (PFP) programme.

"This will be a Turbo-charged PFP with much more consultation and scope for joint exercises, the aim is that eventually there will be little difference between a full member and an active partner," said one official.

In the margins of the meeting, the ministers are set to initial a security pact with Ukraine giving that country a special status above that of partnership, but not going as far as the deal with Russia.

British Foreign Minister Robin Cook said NATO was committed to enlargement eastwards, but gave no clues as to which countries may gain entry at the first attempt -- the alliance's first expansion for two decades.
"We are determined that NATO be widened, we are determined that the new democracies of eastern Europe be able to join the family of democratic nations," he told reporters.

The meeting is also due to review a reform of the alliance's command structures to make it more flexible and allow it to take on more out-of-area peacekeeping peace missions and review its current operation in Bosnia.
